content.text: {"primary_meaning":"In most Christian teaching and biblical interpretation, butter (curds/curdled milk) symbolizes abundance, richness, and the blessing of God's provision — the fatness and prosperity of the land. As a product of pastoral wealth, it stands alongside honey, milk, and oil as an emblem of plenty and divine favor. In the messianic passage Isaiah 7:15 ('Butter and honey shall he eat, that he may know to refuse the evil and choose the good'), it is traditionally applied to the promised child (Immanuel/Christ) and is frequently read as marking his true humanity — that he was nourished on ordinary human food — while interpreters divide over whether the curds-and-honey diet there signals abundance or a reduced subsistence diet after devastation.","primary_basis":["Isaiah 7:15","Isaiah 7:21-22","Genesis 18:8","Deuteronomy 32:13-14","Judges 5:25","2 Samuel 17:29","Job 20:17","Job 29:6"],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"Subsistence or survival food amid desolation: in Isaiah 7:21-22 many modern commentators read curds and honey as the diet of a depopulated land where agriculture has collapsed and only pastoral products remain — a sign of judgment rather than plenty.","basis":["Isaiah 7:15","Isaiah 7:21-25"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Flattering, smooth, or deceitful speech: words 'smoother than butter' while war is in the heart, making butter an image of hypocrisy or treacherous flattery.","basis":["Psalm 55:21"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"The product of pressure or agitation — churning milk produces butter as pressing anger produces strife — used homiletically as an image of how provocation yields conflict, or (positively) how trial produces result.","basis":["Proverbs 30:33"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"Patristic/allegorical readings of Isaiah 7:15: butter and honey as the incarnation — proof of Christ's genuine human flesh and infancy — or allegorized as the sweetness and richness of divine doctrine/the Word.","basis":["Isaiah 7:15","1 Peter 2:2 (by analogy with milk as the word)"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"Hospitality and generous welcome, based on Abraham serving curds to his heavenly visitors and Jael offering curds to Sisera (the latter sometimes read ironically as treacherous hospitality).","basis":["Genesis 18:8","Judges 5:25"],"prominence":"minority"}],"has_settled_consensus":false,"confidence":"medium","notes":"Butter/curds is a comparatively minor biblical image without a single fixed symbolic meaning in the interpretive tradition. The KJV renders the Hebrew 'chemah' as 'butter,' while most modern versions render 'curds,' and the referent is generally understood as curdled milk or a soft dairy product rather than modern churned butter. The abundance/prosperity reading is the most frequently assigned, but Isaiah 7 is genuinely contested (abundance vs. scarcity-after-judgment), and Psalm 55:21's flattery image is an independent, well-recognized figurative use rather than a variant of the same symbol. Because the image splits across these distinct uses, there is recognizable common usage but not a settled, unified symbolic consensus."}
